stem: What is the sum of the series \(0.3 + 0.33 + 0.333 + \cdots\) to \(n\) terms?
solution:
\(S = 0.3 + 0.33 + 0.333 + \cdots\) to \(n\) terms \(= \dfrac{3}{9}\left(0.9 + 0.99 + 0.999 + \cdots\right)\).
\(= \dfrac{1}{3}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{10^{k}}\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}\left[n - \sum_{k=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{10^{k}}\right]\).
The inner sum is a GP with first term \(\dfrac{1}{10}\) and ratio \(\dfrac{1}{10}\): \(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{10^{k}} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{10}\left(1 - \frac{1}{10^{n}}\right)}{1 - \frac{1}{10}} = \dfrac{1}{9}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{10^{n}}\right)\).
\(S = \dfrac{1}{3}\left[n - \dfrac{1}{9}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{10^{n}}\right)\right]\).
Check at \(n = 1\): \(\dfrac{1}{3}\left[1 - \dfrac{1}{9}\left(\dfrac{9}{10}\right)\right] = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{9}{10} = 0.3\).
Matches option A.

stem: If the sum of \(m\) terms of an AP is \(n\) and the sum of \(n\) terms is \(m\), then the sum of \((m + n)\) terms is
solution:
Let the first term be \(a\) and the common difference \(d\).
\(S_{m} = \dfrac{m}{2}\left[2a + (m-1)d\right] = n\) and \(S_{n} = \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a + (n-1)d\right] = m\).
Multiplying out and subtracting: \((m-n)\left[2a + (m+n-1)d\right] = 2(n-m)\).
Dividing by \(m-n\): \(2a + (m+n-1)d = -2\).
\(S_{m+n} = \dfrac{m+n}{2}\left[2a + (m+n-1)d\right] = \dfrac{m+n}{2}(-2)\).
\(= -(m+n)\).
Matches option D.

stem: The sum of the roots of the equation \(x^{2} + bx + c = 0\) (where \(b\) and \(c\) are non-zero) is equal to the sum of the reciprocals of their squares. Then \(\frac{1}{c},\ b,\ \frac{c}{b}\) are in
solution:
Let the roots be \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), so \(\alpha + \beta = -b\) and \(\alpha\beta = c\).
The condition is \(\alpha + \beta = \dfrac{1}{\alpha^{2}} + \dfrac{1}{\beta^{2}} = \dfrac{(\alpha+\beta)^{2} - 2\alpha\beta}{(\alpha\beta)^{2}}\).
\(-b = \dfrac{b^{2} - 2c}{c^{2}}\), so \(-bc^{2} = b^{2} - 2c\), giving \(b^{2} + bc^{2} = 2c\).
Now test the three quantities \(\dfrac{1}{c},\ b,\ \dfrac{c}{b}\) for harmonic progression: their reciprocals \(c,\ \dfrac{1}{b},\ \dfrac{b}{c}\) are in arithmetic progression exactly when \(\dfrac{2}{b} = c + \dfrac{b}{c}\).
Clearing the denominators gives \(2c = bc^{2} + b^{2}\), which is precisely the relation already obtained, so the three quantities are in harmonic progression.
Check with \(b = -2,\ c = 1\): \(x^{2} - 2x + 1 = 0\) has roots \(1\) and \(1\), whose sum is \(2\) and whose reciprocal squares also total \(2\); the three quantities are then \(1,\ -2,\ -\dfrac{1}{2}\), whose reciprocals \(1,\ -\dfrac{1}{2},\ -2\) fall by \(\dfrac{3}{2}\) each step.
Matches option C.

stem: The fifth term of an AP of \(n\) terms, whose sum is \(n^{2} - 2n\), is
solution:
Given \(S_{n} = n^{2} - 2n\).
A term is the difference of consecutive sums: \(a_{5} = S_{5} - S_{4}\).
\(S_{5} = 25 - 10 = 15\) and \(S_{4} = 16 - 8 = 8\).
\(a_{5} = 15 - 8 = 7\).
Matches option B.

stem: The sum of the first \(n\) terms of the series \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{3}{4} + \frac{7}{8} + \frac{15}{16} + \cdots\) is equal to
solution:
The \(k\)th term is \(\dfrac{2^{k}-1}{2^{k}} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{2^{k}}\).
\(S_{n} = \sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2^{k}}\right) = n - \sum_{k=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{2^{k}}\).
The GP sums to \(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{2^{k}} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{2^{n}}\).
\(S_{n} = n - 1 + 2^{-n}\).
Check at \(n = 2\): \(2 - 1 + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{5}{4}\), and \(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{5}{4}\).
Matches option C.

stem: If \(S_{n} = nP + \frac{n(n-1)Q}{2}\), where \(S_{n}\) denotes the sum of the first \(n\) terms of an AP, then the common difference is
solution:
For an AP, \(S_{n} = na + \dfrac{n(n-1)d}{2}\).
Comparing term by term with \(S_{n} = nP + \dfrac{n(n-1)Q}{2}\) gives \(a = P\) and \(d = Q\).
Check directly: \(a_{1} = S_{1} = P\), and \(a_{2} = S_{2} - S_{1} = (2P + Q) - P = P + Q\).
\(d = a_{2} - a_{1} = Q\).
Matches option D.

stem: The value of the product \(6^{\frac{1}{2}} \times 6^{\frac{1}{4}} \times 6^{\frac{1}{8}} \times 6^{\frac{1}{16}} \times \ldots\) up to infinite terms is
solution:
The product is \(6^{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{16} + \cdots}\), since multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents.
The exponent is an infinite GP with first term \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) and ratio \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).
Its sum is \(\dfrac{1/2}{1 - 1/2} = 1\).
The product is \(6^{1} = 6\).
Matches option A.

stem: If \(y = x + x^{2} + x^{3} + \cdots\) up to infinite terms, where \(x < 1\), then which one of the following is correct?
solution:
\(y = x + x^{2} + x^{3} + \cdots\) is an infinite GP with first term \(x\) and ratio \(x\).
\(y = \dfrac{x}{1-x}\).
\(y(1-x) = x\), so \(y = x + xy\) and \(y = x(1+y)\).
\(x = \dfrac{y}{1+y}\).
Matches option A.

stem: If \(1 \cdot 3 + 2 \cdot 3^{2} + 3 \cdot 3^{3} + \cdots + n \cdot 3^{n} = \frac{(2n-1)3^{a} + b}{4}\), then \(a\) and \(b\) are respectively
solution:
Let \(S = 1\cdot3 + 2\cdot3^{2} + 3\cdot3^{3} + \cdots + n\cdot3^{n}\).
Then \(3S = 1\cdot3^{2} + 2\cdot3^{3} + \cdots + n\cdot3^{n+1}\).
Subtracting, \(S - 3S = 3 + 3^{2} + \cdots + 3^{n} - n\cdot3^{n+1}\), so \(-2S = \dfrac{3\left(3^{n}-1\right)}{2} - n\cdot3^{n+1}\).
\(S = \dfrac{n\cdot3^{n+1}}{2} - \dfrac{3^{n+1}-3}{4} = \dfrac{2n\cdot3^{n+1} - 3^{n+1} + 3}{4}\).
\(S = \dfrac{(2n-1)3^{n+1} + 3}{4}\), so the exponent is \(n+1\) and the added term is \(3\).
Check at \(n = 2\): the left side is \(3 + 18 = 21\), and \(\dfrac{3 \times 27 + 3}{4} = \dfrac{84}{4} = 21\).
Matches option D.

stem: If \(x = 1 - y + y^{2} - y^{3} + \cdots\) where \(|y| < 1\), then which is correct?
solution:
\(x = 1 - y + y^{2} - y^{3} + \cdots\) is an infinite GP with first term \(1\) and ratio \(-y\).
Since \(|y| < 1\), the ratio satisfies \(|-y| < 1\) and the series converges.
\(x = \dfrac{1}{1 - (-y)}\).
\(= \dfrac{1}{1+y}\).
Matches option A.

stem: The sum of the series \(3 - 1 + \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{9} + \cdots\) is equal to
solution:
The series is a GP with first term \(3\) and ratio \(r = -\dfrac{1}{3}\), since each term is the previous one divided by \(-3\).
\(|r| < 1\), so the infinite sum exists: \(S_{\infty} = \dfrac{a}{1-r}\).
\(= \dfrac{3}{1 + \frac{1}{3}} = \dfrac{3}{\frac{4}{3}}\).
\(= \dfrac{9}{4}\).
Matches option C.

stem: If an infinite GP has the first term \(x\) and the sum 5, then which one of the following is correct?
solution:
\(S_{\infty} = \dfrac{x}{1-r} = 5\), so \(1 - r = \dfrac{x}{5}\) and \(r = 1 - \dfrac{x}{5}\).
An infinite GP has a sum only when \(|r| < 1\): \(-1 < 1 - \dfrac{x}{5} < 1\).
Subtracting 1 throughout: \(-2 < -\dfrac{x}{5} < 0\), so \(0 < \dfrac{x}{5} < 2\).
\(0 < x < 10\).
Both ends are genuinely excluded: \(x = 0\) would make every term zero, and \(x = 10\) would give \(r = -1\), for which the series does not converge.
Matches option C.

stem: If the second term of a GP is 2 and the sum of its infinite terms is 8, then the GP is
solution:
Given \(ar = 2\) and \(\dfrac{a}{1-r} = 8\).
Substituting \(a = \dfrac{2}{r}\) into the second: \(\dfrac{2}{r(1-r)} = 8\), so \(8r - 8r^{2} = 2\).
\(4r^{2} - 4r + 1 = 0\), that is \((2r-1)^{2} = 0\), so \(r = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and this is the only possible ratio.
\(a = \dfrac{2}{r} = 4\), so the progression is \(4, 2, 1, \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{4}, \ldots\)
Check: its second term is \(2\) and its sum is \(\dfrac{4}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} = 8\).
Matches option C.

stem: What is the \(n^{th}\) term of the sequence \(25, -125, 625, -3125, \ldots\)?
solution:
Writing the terms as powers of 5: \(25 = 5^{2}\), \(-125 = -5^{3}\), \(625 = 5^{4}\), \(-3125 = -5^{5}\).
The magnitude of the \(n\)th term is therefore \(5^{n+1}\).
The signs run \(+, -, +, -\), starting positive, which is \((-1)^{n-1}\).
\(a_{n} = (-1)^{n-1}5^{n+1}\).
Check: \(n = 1\) gives \(5^{2} = 25\) and \(n = 2\) gives \(-5^{3} = -125\).
The forms carrying \((-1)^{2n}\) and \((-1)^{2n-1}\) have even and odd exponents respectively, so they are always \(+1\) and always \(-1\) and never alternate.
Matches option D.

stem: What is the value of \(1 - 2 + 3 - 4 + 5 - \cdots + 101\) ?
solution:
Group the terms in pairs from the start: \((1-2) + (3-4) + \cdots + (99-100) + 101\).
Each bracket equals \(-1\), and the numbers 1 to 100 form \(50\) such pairs.
The last term \(101\) is odd and is left over unpaired.
Sum \(= 50 \times (-1) + 101 = -50 + 101\).
\(= 51\).
Matches option A.

stem: Let \(S_{n}\) be the sum of the first \(n\) terms of an AP. If \(S_{2n} = 3n + 14n^{2}\), then what is the common difference ?
solution:
Put \(m = 2n\), so \(n = \dfrac{m}{2}\) and \(S_{m} = 3\left(\dfrac{m}{2}\right) + 14\left(\dfrac{m}{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{3m}{2} + \dfrac{7m^{2}}{2}\).
For an AP, \(S_{m} = \dfrac{d}{2}m^{2} + \left(a - \dfrac{d}{2}\right)m\).
Comparing the coefficients of \(m^{2}\): \(\dfrac{d}{2} = \dfrac{7}{2}\).
\(d = 7\).
Check: the coefficients of \(m\) give \(a - \dfrac{7}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2}\), so \(a = 5\); then \(S_{2} = 5 + 12 = 17\), which matches \(3(1) + 14(1) = 17\).
Matches option C.

stem: If \(x^{2},\ x,\ -8\) are in AP, then which one of the following is correct?
solution:
Three quantities are in AP when the middle one is the average of the outer two: \(2x = x^{2} + (-8)\).
\(x^{2} - 2x - 8 = 0\).
\((x-4)(x+2) = 0\), so \(x = 4\) or \(x = -2\).
Both values genuinely work: \(x = 4\) gives \(16, 4, -8\) with common difference \(-12\), and \(x = -2\) gives \(4, -2, -8\) with common difference \(-6\), so neither root may be discarded.
Matches option C.

stem: If the sum of the first 9 terms of an AP is equal to sum of the first 11 terms, then what is the sum of the first 20 terms?
solution:
\(S_{9} = S_{11}\) means the tenth and eleventh terms together contribute nothing: \(a_{10} + a_{11} = 0\).
\(S_{20} = \dfrac{20}{2}\left(a_{1} + a_{20}\right) = 10\left(a_{1} + a_{20}\right)\).
In an AP two terms whose subscripts add to the same total have the same sum, and \(1 + 20 = 10 + 11 = 21\), so \(a_{1} + a_{20} = a_{10} + a_{11}\).
\(S_{20} = 10 \times 0 = 0\).
Matches option D.

stem: If the 5th term of an AP is \(\frac{1}{10}\) and its 10th term is \(\frac{1}{5}\), then what is the sum of first 50 terms?
solution:
\(a + 4d = \dfrac{1}{10}\) and \(a + 9d = \dfrac{1}{5}\).
Subtracting: \(5d = \dfrac{1}{5} - \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{1}{10}\), so \(d = \dfrac{1}{50}\).
\(a = \dfrac{1}{10} - 4\left(\dfrac{1}{50}\right) = \dfrac{5-4}{50} = \dfrac{1}{50}\).
\(S_{50} = \dfrac{50}{2}\left[2a + 49d\right] = 25\left[\dfrac{2}{50} + \dfrac{49}{50}\right] = 25 \times \dfrac{51}{50}\).
\(= \dfrac{51}{2} = 25.5\).
Matches option B.

stem: The sum of all the two-digit odd numbers is
solution:
The two-digit odd numbers are \(11, 13, 15, \ldots, 99\), an AP with \(a = 11\) and \(d = 2\).
\(99 = 11 + (n-1)2\) gives \(n - 1 = 44\), so \(n = 45\).
\(S = \dfrac{n}{2}\left(\text{first} + \text{last}\right) = \dfrac{45}{2}(11 + 99)\).
\(= \dfrac{45}{2} \times 110 = 45 \times 55 = 2475\).
Matches option A.
